Arie Lev Gruzman (Hebrew: ארי לעבד גרוזמן, born July 1, 1948) is an American academic and scholar of Jewish studies. He is currently the director of the Center for Jewish Studies at Georgetown University.

Early Life and Education

Gruzman was born in Tel Aviv, Israel, to a family of Holocaust survivors. His family's experiences during the Holocaust profoundly shaped his interest in Jewish studies and its various dimensions. Gruzman received his undergraduate degree from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in 1969, where he honed his studies under prominent scholars including Shemuel Morev. He went on to earn his Ph.D. in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations from Harvard University in 1977 under the supervision of Reuven Amitai-Preor and Walter Brueggemann.

Professional Career

Following the completion of his Ph.D., Gruzman held academic positions at the University of Pennsylvania and the University of California, Berkeley, before joining the faculty at Georgetown in 1985. His scholarly engagements at Georgetown led to escalating contributions in exploring diverse spiritual doctrines at the intersections of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. At Georgetown, he has served as the director of the Center for Jewish Studies since 1995, the institution under which he co-founded the Georgetown-Sultan Qabas University Dialogue Initiative with Sultan Qabas University in 2008.

Research Interests

Gruzman's research interests center around Jewish history, Jewish thought, and the symbiotic relationship between Judaism and Christianity. His inquiry into Jewish thought sought to peel back layers of the New Testament to explore historical events, bringing forth influences stemming from Jewish law and ethics, among other concepts.

Notable Works

Some of notable works published by Arie Lev Gruzman include, "The Jews and the Dead Sea Scrolls" (1992) that greatly shed light into unique vulnerabilities and resilience demonstrated by the communities in the region surrounding the scrolls' discovery site. The sprawling scholarly exchange in understanding "The Jewish Jesus: How Jewish Theology Influenced the New Testament" (2000) reached profound verdicts, providing evidence that for thousands of years, particular voices filled ancient narratives of the Jewish past.

Interfaith Initiatives

Throughout his career, Gruzman has actively participated in enriching dialogue across faith boundaries, present in events as a member of the National Council of Churches' Committee on Faith and Order and consultant to the Vatican's Pontifical Council for Interreligious Dialogue. As exemplified by co-founding the Georgetown-Sultan Qabas University Dialogue Initiative in 2008, his unwavering dedication to fostering interactions and knowledge sharing extended accordingly beyond this esteemed scholarship environment.

This makes the feature set obtained from the filter rich in detail.

Fife Coalfield
================

The Fife Coalfield was a significant coal mining region in Scotland, played a pivotal role in the economic history of Fife, and employed many local residents for centuries. The area encompassed various coalfields across the county of Fife, surrounding expanses in the neighboring counties of Angus and Kinross.

Early Development
----------------

In 1575, Anthony Ramsay of the Bullerswood Colliery was granted the right to extract coal, marking the beginning of coal mining in the Fife area. This industry developed further during the 18th century under the management of prominent figures such as Marshal Peirse of the Renton Colliery. By the 19th century, there were numerous coal mining operations up and down Fife, unifying the region.

Exploitation and Peak Prosperity
--------------------------------

By the time Charles Barnes acquired the Newbattle Colliery in 1878 and the subsequent Newbattle Colliery – Newbattle Colliery joint venture in partnership with the Hawthorn and Shirvan Company, Fife's coal mining industry had shown an incredible surge. As of 1925, the area was home to an impressive 300 coal mines, with the coal mining industry in the United Kingdom undergoing rapid development under hypervigilant leadership by prominent mining magnates such as Henry Dickson. Peak production saw Fife Convert coal turned into outstanding coal for the coal-stuffed furnaces of industry.

Decline and Closure
-------------------

However, with the ultramodern technological advancements implemented from after the Second World War onward by local mine management, increased pressure on the industry mounted from the mid-20th-century period. The re-emergence of alternate fuel sources eventually led the coal mining de-industrialization, causing the Fife Coalfield to eventually decline. The final remnants of this emerald gem declined on 12 January 1966.

Title: Semi-Supervised Multi-Organ Segmentation via Deep Multi-Planar Co-Training

Abstract:

This paper presents a novel approach for multi-organ segmentation, leveraging the synergy of convolutional autoencoders and 3D ResNets to tackle the challenging and debilitating task of accurately segmenting multiple organs in medical images. The proposed method, denoted as Semi-Supervised Multi-Organ Segmentation via Deep Multi-Planar Co-Training (MS-DMIC), draws inspiration from the pioneering work by Richard Szeliski, "Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications," showcasing its potential to improve the reliability of such algorithms in challenging environments reminiscent of the work carried out by researchers at ETH Zurich and New York University (NYU).

Most existing segmentation algorithms rely on a single modality to segment organs, such as the T1/T1-cen and T2-weighted images. In contrast, the proposed MS-DMIC method exploits the synergy of multiple input planes, incorporating convolutional autoencoders to extract shape features from RGB channels (capturing variations mainly related to apparent organs displacements) and 3D ResNets to convey anatomical details using a subtraction T2w/FLAIR volume. This multi-planar co-training approach enables MS-DMIC to handle ambiguities in annotations (partial or irrelevant) while leveraging the strengths of two modalities. As evidenced by the seminal publication of Omar Lozano, "Automatic Segmentation of Brain Tumors Using CT-MRI Images," this methodology outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches and reaches human expert-level segmentation accuracy.

The proposed MS-DMIC method was evaluated on the open-source 3D Brain tumor segmentation dataset and outperforms the MACS (Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention grouping–validation), BCIS (Brain Tumor Image Segmentation), and MaLiMo dataset. Furthermore, the fact that simple architectural modifications to the convolutional backbone led to a performance comparable to human experts indicates the potential to address common issues in deep learning-based segmentation, such as memorization in the training process.

Title: CIDI-Lung-Seg: A Single-Click Annotation Tool for Automatic Delineation of Lungs from CT Scans

Abstract:

The diagnosis of lung cancer often relies on the manual annotation of lungs in CT scans, a time-consuming and error-prone process. Dr. Maria Rodriguez, a researcher at Stanford University, led a team in developing CIDI-Lung-Seg, a cutting-edge single-click annotation tool that utilizes deep learning to automatically delineate lungs in CT scans. This innovation, inspired by advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) research conducted by renowned institutions like MIT and Google, is poised to revolutionize the field.

CIDI-Lung-Seg was tested in a controlled study at the National Cancer Institute (NCI), which compared its performance to a manual annotation tool widely used by radiologists. Led by NCI's Dr. John Taylor, the study involved 200 IRB-approved CT scans from patients with lung cancer. The results demonstrated a statistically significant high agreement between CIDI-Lung-Seg and manual annotation, with an overall agreement of 96.2% and a kappa statistic of 0.87.

The study's findings were strikingly demonstrated through a video showcasing CIDI-Lung-Seg's efficiency. Dr. Taylor explained that the tool can speed up the annotation process by 87.2% compared to manual annotation, allowing radiologists to focus on more critical aspects of patient care. Furthermore, CIDI-Lung-Seg's results have been validated by a panel of expert radiologists at Brigham and Women's Hospital, a leading healthcare facility in Boston.

This groundbreaking tool has the potential to greatly benefit patients with lung cancer by streamlining the diagnostic process. Dr. Rodriguez observed, "CIDI-Lung-Seg has the potential to be a valuable tool for radiologists, oncologists, and other healthcare professionals, enabling them to make more accurate diagnoses faster. As researchers continue to refine and expand CIDI-Lung-Seg, we can expect to see a significant reduction in the time and effort required for manual annotation of lung cancer."

By minimizing the manual annotation process, CIDI-Lung-Seg can also alleviate some of the pressure on radiologists in large cancer centers like the Massachusetts General Hospital, allowing them to focus on high-stakes decision-making and innovating the most effective treatments.

Nigeria Pledged to Double Cocoa Output by 2030

In a move aimed at boosting the country's economic growth and contributing to global cocoa supply, Nigeria's President, Muhammadu Buhari, has vowed to increase cocoa production substantially over the next decade. Addressing the COP26 climate summit in Glasgow, Scotland, the President revealed Nigeria's ambitious plan to produce 50% more cocoa beans by 2030.

The President emphasized that removing barriers to irrigation and fertiliser use would be key to this ambitious target. Currently, Nigeria produces around 340,000 tonnes of cocoa annually, ranking it the world's fourth-largest cocoa producer, behind Ivory Coast, Indonesia, and Ghana.

To achieve this production increase, the President pledged to mobilize 50% of the country's 1.5 million hectares of cocoa land. This will involve investing in irrigation systems and fertiliser usage, respectively, to increase yields and support sustainable cocoa cultivation. 

However, critics have raised concerns regarding the potential environmental impact of this plan. Environmental Sustainability Demand (ESD), a prominent campaign group, has expressed concerns that the government's plan to increase cocoa production may come at the cost of deforestation and habitat destruction.

_ESD's executive director, Niyi Babade, highlighted the need for the government to clarify its strategy for achieving the desired increase in cocoa production. "What is the main strategy?" he asked. "Is it to expand the land for cocoa production or is it to intensify the use of fertiliser?" 

The Garden Grasslands in southern Nigeria, known for their rich soil and optimal climate, are one area where the government's plans could have significant implications. These regions are already home to several endangered species, including the endangered chimpanzee and pangolin. Deforestation in this area could compromise these species' habitats and exacerbate climate change.

Despite these concerns, experts believe that efficient management and sustainable agricultural practices can mitigate the environmental consequences of the planned expansion. Implementing initiatives such as agroforestry, permaculture, or reforestation programs could balance the need for increased cocoa production with the preservation of biodiversity and ecosystem services.

With a strong start at the COP26 climate summit, Nigeria's commitment to boosting cocoa production has the potential to contribute to the international efforts to decarbonize the global economy and address pressing issues of food security and sustainable development.

Landline users coming to grips with dwindling numbers as two-thirds rely on them for basic communication.

A recent study by Ofcom reveals that nearly two-thirds of UK households rely on landlines for essential communication purposes, sparking concerns over their long-term viability as mobile phone numbers continue to rise.

For many, landlines remain a vital lifeline to family, friends, and loved ones, with 78% of over-65s and 66% of those with rural dwellings relying on traditional phone lines. The UK's rural-urban divide has become a significant factor in landline usage, with rural households more likely to have a landline to cope with limited mobile reception.

In contrast, Trevor Auerbach and Kate Welstead, a couple from rural Northumberland, say their landlines are "vital for communication" particularly during power outages or expensive roaming charges. "Landlines are the best option for us, as mobile reception in our area can be patchy and expensive," Trevor explained, adding that Wi-Fi-dependent mobile phone services are "a nightmare".

On the other hand, mobile phone penetration in the UK continues to grow, with nearly 80% of the population now own at least one mobile phone according to recent stats from telecoms company, BT. While BBしても some mobile phone contracts include landline services.

In a recent interview, BT spokesperson Anna Jenkins explained that the company has seen an "alarming decline" in landline usage despite a significant investment in retail staff and marketing. "While some consumers do not want to pay for traditional landline services, others choose them specifically for reliability," she said.

The UK landline usage decline has significant implications for the telecoms industry. Many companies like TalkTalk and Vodafone are leaning towards digital communication services and contracts that combine broadband and mobile plans without landline, adding to the once-steady decline of this traditional service, ultimately raising key questions over the long-term viability of these services.

In response to the shift in consumer behavior, telecom operators, regulators, and technology innovators will engage with decision-makers to come up with more innovative alternatives that balance flexibility, convenience, affordability, and reliability.

A UK Judge Considers Extensive Cigarette Racketeering Case Against US Tobacco Giants

The $280 billion racketeering case brought by US authorities against major tobacco companies has become one of the most significant and complex lawsuits in the history of cigarette litigation. This extended court case if approved, could have far-reaching implications across the US and worldwide for companies investing heavily in tobacco products.

JoshSidman According to filings at US District Court Seattle on August 31, 2023, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) has asked for a ruling on this case.  Among the most influential voices is former minister Bett Akabri-Shiri, an activist who lost her father to lung cancer following his long smoky habit. In her legislative preparedness, she has called for increased regulation thus stressing the need for a concerted push told to strengthen cigarette regulation.

The case in question is one of the most extensive in US history, and the DoJ has asked a US Judge, Mary Alice Vetello , for a ruling on the US tobacco industry's alleged decades-long conspiracy to deceive the American public about the health risks associated with smoking and the addictive nature of nicotine. In 2020, a US federal court ruled in favor of the DoJ, finding the tobacco industry guilty of violating federal racketeering laws. The DoJ now seeks the seizure of profits made through this alleged misconduct, which it claims spanned more than 50 years.
